readings.title: Open Data Structures: A Basic Binary Tree
readings.guidance: Read sections 6.1.1 and 6.1.2 through the recursive height and traversal discussion. Stop before the nonrecursive traversal. Write the empty-tree return value and the fact each recursive call returns to its parent.
readings.supports: recursive subtree contracts, height, traversal cost, and call-stack depth

readings.title: Reasoning About Recursive Tree Traversals
readings.guidance: Read the abstract, section 1, and section 2.1's traversal examples. Stop before the logical encoding. Track how recursive invocations and the call stack identify the current subtree.
readings.supports: recursive subtree invocations, traversal order, call-stack state, and dependencies between visits

readings.title: Stanford CS106B: Binary Trees, Binary Search Trees, and Tree Traversals
readings.guidance: Read Binary Trees and the TreeNode Struct, then open the linked tree notes and inspect the traversal preview. Focus on left and right child positions and explicit null links.
readings.supports: binary-tree shape, ordered child positions, null structure, and recursive comparison

readings.title: Revisiting Tree Isomorphism: An Algorithmic Bric-a-Brac
readings.guidance: Read the abstract, introduction, and the first formulation of rooted-tree comparison. This paper treats unordered rooted trees, where children may be permuted; the lesson's ordered binary trees keep left and right positions fixed. Use it as an extension of structural comparison, not as the lesson's equality rule.
readings.supports: structural comparison and unambiguous subtree encodings, with an explicit unordered-tree extension beyond ordered binary equality

readings.title: Nick Parlante: Binary Trees
readings.guidance: Read only hasPathSum and printPaths in Section 2, pages 8-10. Trace the root-to-leaf condition and note when a path buffer is copied or restored.
readings.supports: root-to-leaf path semantics, accumulated state, and path output

readings.title: Path and Ancestor Queries over Trees with Multidimensional Weight Vectors
readings.guidance: Read the abstract, introduction, and the definitions of ancestor and path reporting queries. Stop before the data-structure constructions. Treat these queries as a deeper extension of accumulating and reporting values along a root path.
readings.supports: ancestor paths, path aggregation and reporting, output-sensitive cost, and weighted tree paths

readings.title: UC Irvine ICS 46: Tree Traversals
readings.guidance: Read the breadth-first traversal section and its queue trace. Contrast it with preorder and postorder, and record why the queue holds the next level's work.
readings.supports: level-order traversal, FIFO processing, and traversal space

readings.title: Distributed Memory Breadth-First Search Revisited: Enabling Bottom-Up Search
readings.guidance: Read the report abstract and the conventional top-down BFS description in the introduction. Stop before the distributed decomposition. Relate a frontier to one tree level and its maximum size to queue storage.
readings.supports: BFS frontiers, level-by-level discovery, linear traversal bounds, and frontier-width storage

readings.title: Open Data Structures: An Unbalanced Binary Search Tree
readings.guidance: Read search and insertion through section 6.2.2. Track the full ancestor-imposed interval for each recursive descent, then stop before removal.
readings.supports: BST ordering, one-branch search, insertion, height-sensitive cost, and duplicate policy

readings.title: Some Combinatorial Properties of Certain Trees With Applications to Searching and Sorting
readings.guidance: Read the introduction, the binary-search-tree definition on pages 13-14, and section 2.1's search application. Skip the deletion analysis. Note that the paper assumes distinct keys and compare that premise with an explicit duplicate policy.
readings.supports: ordered left and right subtrees, search paths, insertion order, distinct-key assumptions, and expected path length

readings.title: Stanford CS106B: Lowest Common Ancestor in a BST
readings.guidance: Read Problem Three on page 7 only. Use the diagram to check split-subtree and ancestor-as-target cases. Stop before the answer pages; the supplied contract is the reading, not a timed exam.
readings.supports: Defines lowest common ancestors in a binary search tree, including when a target is the ancestor. The ordering permits choosing one subtree until the targets split.

readings.title: The LCA Problem Revisited
readings.guidance: Read the abstract, introduction, and formal problem definition through page 2. Stop before the range-minimum reduction. Compare its preprocessed many-query model with the lesson's one-query recursive and BST-ordering methods.
readings.supports: formal LCA semantics, rooted-tree queries, preprocessing tradeoffs, and constant-time query goals

readings.title: Duke CPS100: Tree Problems
readings.guidance: Read the Tree Diameter problem statement and its three-way recurrence. Write separately what a subtree returns and what contributes to the complete diameter.
readings.supports: postorder height returns, diameter updates, edge counts, and linear traversal

readings.title: Fast Dynamic Programming in Trees in the MPC Model
readings.guidance: Read the abstract and section 1's description of tree dynamic programming and accumulation tasks. Stop before the MPC framework. Use it as a broader extension of combining constant-size child summaries; the introductory reading supplies the exact diameter recurrence.
readings.supports: bottom-up tree dynamic programming, subtree aggregates, constant-size summaries, and diameter-sensitive complexity

readings.title: Jeff Erickson: Backtracking
readings.guidance: Read section 2.1, N Queens, through the generic backtracking pattern. Identify the partial state, legal next choices, base case, and restoration step.
readings.supports: decision trees, legal choices, recursive depth-first search, and reversible mutation

readings.title: Donald Knuth: Dancing Links
readings.guidance: Read the opening two pages and the remove-and-restore equations. Stop before the polyomino experiments. Relate the local undo operation to restoring state before a sibling branch.
readings.supports: reversible local updates, depth-first search, and constraint-guided choice points

readings.title: Stanford CS106B: More Recursion
readings.guidance: Read Recursive Sequence Generation and Recursive Permutation Generation. Compare the state for a position with the state for unused choices, and predict the output counts before tracing code.
readings.supports: sequence and permutation generation, choice position, unused elements, and factorial output

readings.title: Brendan McKay: Backtrack Programming
readings.guidance: Read chapter 6, sections 6.1-6.2, for the formal tree of partial sequences. Stop when the group-theoretic symmetry analysis begins.
readings.supports: enumeration as a tree of partial sequences, distinct choices, and exponential output

readings.title: Stanford CS106B: Recursion and Recursive Backtracking
readings.guidance: Read the permutation-focused Barnstorming problem and its solution. Note why positions are distinct even when a route shares earlier choices, and how state is restored after each candidate.
readings.supports: per-depth choices, used-position state, restoration, and permutation output

readings.title: Generating Permutations of a Bag by Interchanges
readings.guidance: Open the free final-version PDF and read the introduction plus the definition of permutations of a bag. Focus on how repeated values change uniqueness; skip the minimal-change proofs.
readings.supports: unique enumeration when input values repeat and the distinction between positions and values

readings.title: Stanford CS106B: Recursive Backtracking
readings.guidance: Read Win some, lose sum and its recursive solution. Track the remaining choices and current target, then state why each branch either includes or skips one candidate.
readings.supports: sum-search state, include-or-skip branching, termination, and failed-branch pruning

readings.title: Subset Sum in Time 2^(n/2)/poly(n)
readings.guidance: Read the folklore Sorted-Sum-Enumeration algorithm and Lemma 2 on page 5. Ignore the later randomized improvements. Compare duplicate removal with naive subset enumeration.
readings.supports: subset-sum enumeration, duplicate removal, exponential search, and explicit complexity bounds

readings.title: Hunter College: Recursion and Backtracking
readings.guidance: Read the backtracking template and the palindrome material only. Express a string partition state as a consumed prefix and a next boundary; skip grammar material not tied to the search.
readings.supports: recursive string state, palindrome validation, base cases, and backtracking boundaries

readings.title: Palindromic k-Factorization in Pure Linear Time
readings.guidance: Read the abstract, introduction, and problem definition. Stop before the linear-time machinery. Compare complete factorization with accepting a locally palindromic next segment.
readings.supports: whole-string consumption, palindromic factors, required piece counts, and repeated substring checks

readings.title: Stanford CS106B: Boggle
readings.guidance: Read Problem Description and the human word-search requirements. Trace one word while enforcing adjacency and one-use-per-cube; skip the interface and submission sections.
readings.supports: grid adjacency, path-local visited state, exhaustive search, and restoring cells between starts

readings.title: A Computational Proof of the Highest-Scoring Boggle Board
readings.guidance: Read the abstract, introduction, and solver overview. Stop before the board-optimization proof. Focus on how a fast Boggle solver combines trie state, board position, and branch-and-bound search.
readings.supports: grid word search, coupled board and dictionary state, branch pruning, and exhaustive solver structure

readings.title: Stanford CS227: Constraint Reasoning
readings.guidance: Read the CSP definition and backtracking-search slides through variable and value ordering. Record which state facts determine future legal choices; skip local-search methods.
readings.supports: constraint state, legal-choice filtering, search ordering, and pruning

readings.title: Symmetry Breaking Constraints: Recent Results
readings.guidance: Read the abstract, introduction, and the opening value-symmetry example. Stop before row-and-column symmetry. Map interchangeable values to containers with equal current loads.
readings.supports: equivalent branches, value symmetry, canonical representatives, and avoiding repeated search

readings.title: Princeton Algorithms: Undirected Graphs
readings.guidance: Read the graph representation and depth-first search sections. Treat a grid cell as a vertex and legal moves as edges, then identify when a cell becomes marked.
readings.supports: graph modeling, adjacency, discovery-time marking, DFS, and connected components

readings.title: Finding Strong Components Using Depth-First Search
readings.guidance: Read sections 1-2 for the DFS forest, preorder, and active search path. Stop before the strong-component algorithm comparisons.
readings.supports: depth-first traversal, discovery state, linear graph exploration, and component structure

readings.title: Princeton Algorithms: Connected Components Source
readings.guidance: Read the class contract, constructor, and dfs method. Trace how one search labels a whole component and why later starts skip already marked vertices.
readings.supports: component labeling, shared visited state, adjacency-list complexity, and repeated starts

readings.title: Robert Tarjan: Depth-First Search and Linear Graph Algorithms
readings.guidance: Read the abstract and sections 1-2 through the DFS numbering framework. Stop before the biconnected-component proofs. Relate one DFS forest to complete component coverage.
readings.supports: linear-time DFS, component discovery, DFS forests, and traversal state

readings.title: Princeton Algorithms: Breadth-First Paths Source
readings.guidance: Read the class contract and bfs method. Trace mark-on-enqueue, edgeTo, and distTo for one queue layer; skip the test client.
readings.supports: FIFO shortest paths, mark-on-enqueue, distance sentinels, and O(V+E) cost

readings.title: The More the Merrier: Efficient Multi-Source Graph Traversal
readings.guidance: Read the abstract, introduction, and the baseline multi-source BFS description. Stop before vectorized implementation details. Compare simultaneous sources with repeated independent searches.
readings.supports: multi-source BFS, shared frontier work, shortest unweighted distances, and avoiding repeated traversal

readings.title: Stanford CS106B: Graphs
readings.guidance: Read the graph representation and traversal material. For each example, state whether adjacency is stored or generated and whether the goal is reachability or path output.
readings.supports: explicit and implicit adjacency, reachability, traversal state, and path reconstruction

readings.title: PathEnum: Towards Real-Time Hop-Constrained s-t Path Enumeration
readings.guidance: Read the abstract, introduction, and problem definition. Stop before the index construction. Distinguish outputting every source-to-target path from one-time reachability, and note that the paper adds a hop constraint beyond the lesson's DAG setting.
readings.supports: source-to-target path enumeration, depth-first generation, pruning constraints, and output-driven cost

readings.title: Princeton Algorithms: Directed Graphs
readings.guidance: Read Directed cycles and Topological sort. Compare an edge to an active vertex with an edge to a finished vertex, then trace one indegree-based ordering.
readings.supports: directed cycles, active DFS state, topological order, and O(V+E) processing

readings.title: Parameterized Streaming Algorithms for Topological Sorting
readings.guidance: Read the abstract, introduction, and preliminaries' definition of a topological ordering. Stop before the streaming algorithms. Compare the paper's restricted-memory setting with the lesson's in-memory indegree and DFS methods.
readings.supports: topological ordering, directed acyclic graphs, cycle-related applications, and time-space tradeoffs

readings.title: Princeton Algorithms: Union-Find
readings.guidance: Read the connectivity API, weighted quick-union, and path-compression sections. Treat roots as mutable representatives rather than stable component names.
readings.supports: set representatives, union, find, weighting, path compression, and connectivity

readings.title: Robert Tarjan: On the Efficiency of a Good but Not Linear Set Union Algorithm
readings.guidance: Read the repository abstract, then pages 1-3 of the attached technical report for the FIND and UNION model. Stop before the detailed bound proof.
readings.supports: disjoint-set partitions, representatives, path compression, and amortized nonconstant analysis

readings.title: Princeton Algorithms: Shortest Paths
readings.guidance: Read edge relaxation and Dijkstra's algorithm. Stop before all-pairs shortest paths. Record the nonnegative-weight condition and what a priority-queue key means.
readings.supports: weighted relaxation, Dijkstra's frontier, nonnegative weights, stale keys, and complexity

readings.title: E. W. Dijkstra: A Note on Two Problems in Connexion with Graphs
readings.guidance: Read the full three-page paper, focusing on Problem 2 and the permanently labeled nearest node. Translate its positive-length assumption to the lesson's nonnegative-edge condition.
readings.supports: greedy shortest-path finalization, weighted routes, and the edge-weight precondition

readings.title: Open Data Structures: BinaryHeap
readings.guidance: Read the implicit array representation plus add and remove. Trace one bubble-up and one bubble-down, then stop before heapsort.
readings.supports: heap order, array representation, root access, insertion, removal, and O(log n) updates

readings.title: The Best Case of Heapsort
readings.guidance: Read the abstract and opening description of the heap-ordered complete tree. Stop before the best-case comparison proofs. Note what heap order does and does not say about siblings.
readings.supports: heap-ordered complete trees, array layout, heap construction, and partial rather than total order

readings.title: Cornell CS2112: Priority Queues and Heaps
readings.guidance: Read the priority-queue abstraction and heap invariant through bubble up and bubble down. Write the priority as a comparison function over the full item, including ties.
readings.supports: derived priorities, heap comparators, total ordering, and exposing the most extreme item

readings.title: Fibonacci Heaps and Their Uses in Improved Network Optimization Algorithms
readings.guidance: Read the abstract and section 1's heap interface. Stop before the Fibonacci-heap structure. Note that the queue orders items by keys and exposes only the minimum item.
readings.supports: top-k selection, heap-ordered candidates, output-sensitive cost, and ranked frontiers

readings.title: Jeff Erickson: Greedy Algorithms
readings.guidance: Read the opening greedy-framework discussion and its first exchange argument. Stop after ten minutes. State the exchange that replaces a chosen smaller frequency group with a larger one.
readings.supports: greedy choice, exchange arguments, sorted priorities, and proof obligations

readings.title: Greedy Algorithms and Poset Matroids
readings.guidance: Read the introduction, Algorithm 1, and Theorem 1.1 only. Treat choosing at most k frequency groups as the simple cardinality-constrained case, then specialize the maximum-weight choice to largest frequency first.
readings.supports: maximum-weight greedy selection, descending priorities, exchange structure, and the boundary where greedy needs proof

readings.title: Princeton Algorithms: Multiway Merge Source
readings.guidance: Read the class contract and merge method. Track the source index stored with each heap item and explain why only that source advances after a deletion.
readings.supports: one-candidate-per-stream frontiers, source advancement, and O(k log r) merging

readings.title: Selection from Heaps, Row-Sorted Matrices and X+Y Using Soft Heaps
readings.guidance: Read the row-sorted-matrix and X+Y problem statements plus the collection-of-sorted-lists result. Stop before the soft-heap proof. Relate each active row to a frontier candidate.
readings.supports: k-way sorted frontiers, row-sorted selection, pair-sum selection, and output-sensitive bounds

readings.title: Carnegie Mellon 15-122: Multi-Way Tries
readings.guidance: Read sections 2-3 on pages 1-3. Focus on character edges, terminal markers, lookup cost, and why a stored word may have descendants; skip binary and ternary tries.
readings.supports: prefix nodes, terminal markers, exact lookup, prefix lookup, and O(L) operations

readings.title: Fast Algorithms for Sorting and Searching Strings
readings.guidance: Read the abstract, introduction, and section 3 through the ternary-search-tree lookup description. Stop before experiments and advanced query types.
readings.supports: character-directed search, prefix sharing, string-key lookup, and space tradeoffs

readings.title: Princeton Algorithms: Tries
readings.guidance: Read R-way tries, prefix matching, and ordered operations. Compare a trie walk with sorting keys and finding the contiguous prefix range; stop before substring search.
readings.supports: prefix queries, lexicographic traversal, terminal-prefix stopping, and static alternatives

readings.title: Efficient Trie-Based Sorting of Large Sets of Strings
readings.guidance: Read the introduction and the trie-based sorting description. Focus on how trie traversal emits lexicographic order and how child representation changes space use; skip the benchmark tables.
readings.supports: lexicographic string search, prefix descendants, wildcard branching, and ordered output

readings.title: University of Maryland: Heaps and Priority Queue
readings.guidance: Read the scheduling example and the priority-queue operations through the heap representation. Separate a task's release or deadline from its comparator priority.
readings.supports: task availability, scheduling priority, heap selection, and tie rules

readings.title: On-line Scheduling to Minimize Average Completion Time Revisited
readings.guidance: Read the abstract and section 1 through the online scheduling model. Stop before the competitive analysis. Separate each job's release date from the priority ratio used after it becomes available.
readings.supports: release times, eligible-job selection, scheduling priorities, and online idle-versus-work decisions
